title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Hospital destination may be associated with outcomes after a heart failure readmission.



To evaluate the association between different-hospital first readmission and a composite of death during that readmission or subsequent all-cause inpatient admission after live discharge.



We studied adults with a principal-diagnosis heart failure discharge in January through October and a first all-cause readmission within 30 days in the 2016–2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database. Exposure was readmission at the same versus a different hospital. The primary outcome was death during the first readmission or, among survivors, readmission within 30 days after discharge. Survey-weighted regression and design-based standardization estimated adjusted risks and risk differences.



Among 518,986 eligible first readmissions (509,293 in the complete-case adjusted analysis), the adjusted composite risk was 35.6% (95% CI, 35.5–35.8) after same-hospital and 37.6% (95% CI, 37.3–38.0) after different-hospital readmission; the risk difference was +2.00 percentage points (95% CI, +1.64 to +2.36) and the risk ratio was 1.06, 95% CI 1.05–1.07. The adjusted risks were 6.1% (95% CI, 6.0–6.2) versus 7.4% (95% CI, 7.2–7.6) for in-hospital death (risk ratio, 1.21, 95% CI 1.17–1.24) and 31.5% (95% CI, 31.3–31.6) versus 32.7% (95% CI, 32.3–33.0) for subsequent readmission among survivors (risk difference, +1.20 percentage points (95% CI, +0.84 to +1.56); risk ratio, 1.04, 95% CI 1.03–1.05). Different-hospital readmission increased from 20.7% in 2016 to 23.2% in 2022.



Different-hospital first readmission was associated with a modestly higher composite risk, with the largest relative association for death during the first readmission. These findings are associational and do not establish an effect of hospital destination.

title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Introduction
Heart failure hospitalization is often followed by additional inpatient care. Prior studies have compared outcomes for patients readmitted to the original or a different hospital [1,2], and national studies have described repeated admissions after heart failure hospitalization [4]. Studies of interhospital care fragmentation provide broader context [3,5]. This study extends that literature by examining the first all-cause readmission after a heart failure admission and the subsequent inpatient course. A different hospital is an administrative site distinction in the Nationwide Readmissions Database; it does not establish fragmented clinician care, information exchange, transfer appropriateness, or care quality.

title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Methods

Data source and cohort
We used the 2016–2022 Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD), a weighted sample of inpatient stays that supports patient linkage within a state and calendar year. We identified adults aged 18 years or older discharged from January through October after a principal-diagnosis heart failure admission. One eligible index admission was retained per patient-year. Sequential exclusions were age younger than 18 years; index in-hospital death or unknown status; transfer to acute care; discharge against medical advice; non-resident status; missing linkage, hospital identifier, or length of stay; same-day or rehabilitation events; and later ineligible index admissions. We then selected the first all-cause readmission within 30 days; heart failure was not required as the readmission diagnosis. The earliest event was selected by days from index discharge, with ties on the same NRD day resolved by the NRD event key; ties were counted once per year (Table 0). The first linked event defined eligibility: if it was same-day-collapsed, a rehabilitation transfer, or an acute-care transfer, the index admission was excluded, with no search for a later qualifying event. Patients entered the cohort whether or not they survived that readmission. To keep 30-day follow-up within the same calendar year, the first-readmission discharge month had to be November or earlier; this rule applied symmetrically to known-status deaths and live discharges, excluding both after-November survivors and deaths.


Exposure and outcome hierarchy
The exposure was a first all-cause readmission at a different hospital versus the index hospital, determined by the NRD hospital identifier within year. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital death during the first readmission or, among patients discharged alive, any inpatient readmission within 30 days of that discharge. The primary denominator included first readmissions with known vital status. Key secondary outcomes were in-hospital death during the first readmission and subsequent readmission among patients discharged alive. Other secondary outcomes were first-readmission length of stay and hospitalization cost, HF-coded subsequent readmission, and non-elective-coded subsequent readmission.


Covariates and statistical analysis
The congestive heart failure comorbidity indicator was omitted because nearly all patients had it. The primary adjustment set included discharge year; age; sex; expected payer; ZIP-code income quartile; county urban–rural category; index-hospital bed size, location/teaching status, ownership, and annual heart failure volume; index length of stay; index discharge disposition; All Patient Refined Diagnosis Related Groups (APR-DRG) severity; Elixhauser comorbidities; days from index discharge to first readmission (1–7, 8–14, or 15–30); and any earlier hospitalization in the calendar year when derivable. Annual heart-failure volume counted all principal-diagnosis HF discharges across all months and ages within each hospital-year; quartiles were assigned once per unique hospital-year, with tied volumes ordered by hospital identifier when a cutpoint split a tie. Age and log(1+index length of stay) used natural splines with boundary knots at the 5th/95th percentiles and internal knots at the 35th/65th percentiles in the primary complete-case population; numeric knots are listed in Table S4. Adjustment was restricted to information measured before the first-readmission destination; first-readmission length of stay, severity, procedures, and receiving-hospital characteristics were excluded from the primary model.
We used survey-weighted logistic regression with year-specific strata and primary sampling units, nested design handling, and domain estimation. Survey-design delta-method standardization estimated adjusted risks and 95% confidence intervals. The primary contrast was the risk difference (different hospital minus same hospital), reported in percentage points; the risk ratio was secondary. We used overlap weights from a propensity score based on the primary covariates, multiplied by the survey weight, as a sensitivity analysis and summarized covariate balance before and after weighting. Prespecified subgroup estimates were examined by age, sex, payer, rurality, index-hospital location/teaching category, and first-readmission cause; exposure-by-subgroup Wald tests assessed interaction. These subgroup analyses were exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Annual destination proportions and outcome contrasts were assessed with year as a continuous term for trend tests.
Hospitalization cost was derived as total charges multiplied by the NRD cost-to-charge ratio, then inflated to 2022 US dollars using the Consumer Price Index for medical care. Missing total charges and invalid cost-to-charge ratios were excluded from cost analyses; charge-missing exclusions are reported in Table 4. Length of stay, including zero-day stays, and cost were modeled with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson regression using a log link; adjusted ratios of means and 95% confidence intervals are reported with weighted means and medians. Missing covariate data were preserved in the primary data and handled by complete-case analysis; the missing-category sensitivity coded categorical missing values as Unknown. Missingness by variable and exposure, and complete-case inclusion by exposure and year, are summarized in the supplement. The elective-readmission sensitivity excluded records coded elective and records with missing elective status; its denominator is reported in Table 6. First-readmission cause in the destination-predictor model is a concurrent correlate measured during that stay, not an antecedent predictor. Cells with counts of 10 or fewer are shown as ≤10; associated percentages and the minimum complementary cells are suppressed. All analyses use deidentified administrative data and report associations in a selected cohort; they do not estimate causal effects.

title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Results

Cohort and baseline characteristics
The analytic cohort included 518,986 first readmissions: 407,149 same-hospital and 111,837 different-hospital readmissions. The primary complete-case model included 400,239 same-hospital and 109,054 different-hospital readmissions. Table 0 presents each sequential exclusion, including unknown first-readmission vital status, discharge after November, same-day events, rehabilitation, acute-care transfer, and complete-case loss. Earliest-readmission date ties resolved by the NRD event key occurred 0 times across the seven years.
Patients with different-hospital readmission were younger, more often covered by Medicaid, more often lived in non-metropolitan counties, and more often had their index HF admission at a small hospital. Table 1 summarizes the analytic cohort using survey-weighted percentages, unweighted counts, and standardized mean differences; no baseline significance tests were performed.


Primary and secondary outcomes
The adjusted primary composite risks were 35.6% (95% CI, 35.5–35.8) after same-hospital and 37.6% (95% CI, 37.3–38.0) after different-hospital readmission, with a risk difference of +2.00 percentage points (95% CI, +1.64 to +2.36) and risk ratio of 1.06, 95% CI 1.05–1.07. In-hospital death risks were 6.1% (95% CI, 6.0–6.2) versus 7.4% (95% CI, 7.2–7.6); the adjusted risk difference was +1.26 percentage points (95% CI, +1.06 to +1.45) and risk ratio was 1.21, 95% CI 1.17–1.24. Among patients discharged alive, subsequent admission risks were 31.5% (95% CI, 31.3–31.6) versus 32.7% (95% CI, 32.3–33.0), with a risk difference of +1.20 percentage points (95% CI, +0.84 to +1.56) and risk ratio of 1.04, 95% CI 1.03–1.05.
The adjusted HF-coded subsequent-readmission risk difference was +0.18 percentage points (95% CI, -0.07 to +0.42) (P = 0.157). The adjusted risk difference for non-elective-coded subsequent readmission was +0.94 percentage points (95% CI, +0.59 to +1.29). Unadjusted estimates and denominators are shown in Table 2; adjusted estimates and outcome-specific analysis populations are shown in Table 3.


Resource use, causes, and additional analyses
Table 4 reports survey-weighted median (IQR) and mean resource use by exposure, the unweighted and weighted denominators, and adjusted ratios of means. Zero-day stays were included in length-of-stay analyses; missing charges and invalid cost-to-charge ratios were excluded from cost analyses. AKI denotes acute kidney injury and GI denotes gastrointestinal. First-readmission causes are assigned once using the ordered, mutually exclusive ICD-10-CM map in Table S8; pneumonia is classified under respiratory disease and R06 under respiratory/chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Subgroup risk differences and interaction tests are shown in Table 5b; these analyses are exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Sensitivity risk differences ranged from +1.94 to +2.32 percentage points. After overlap weighting, the maximum absolute standardized difference among propensity-model covariates was 0.004; the weighted risk difference is shown in Table 6. Annual weighted different-hospital readmission increased from 20.7% in 2016 to 23.2% in 2022 (P < 0.001); the trend in annual risk differences was P = 0.070. Figure 4 shows annual estimates.

title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Discussion
In this contemporary national cohort, different-hospital first readmission was associated with a modestly higher adjusted risk of the primary composite. Prior HF studies also reported worse outcomes for patients readmitted to a different hospital, particularly mortality and length of stay during that encounter [1,2]. The strongest relative association in this analysis was with in-hospital death during the first readmission (adjusted risk ratio, 1.21, 95% CI 1.17–1.24); the subsequent-admission difference after live discharge was +1.20 percentage points (95% CI, +0.84 to +1.56). HF-coded subsequent readmission showed an adjusted risk difference of +0.18 percentage points (95% CI, -0.07 to +0.42). Different-hospital readmission increased over the study period, from 20.7% to 23.2%. Subgroup estimates and interaction tests are shown in Table 5b and require confirmation.
These findings should be interpreted as associations. The cohort was selected on experiencing a first readmission, and the post-discharge outcome additionally conditions on live discharge. Conditioning on these events can introduce selection bias. NRD hospital identifiers capture site, not clinician continuity or information exchange, and the database does not measure distance, referral, ambulance routing, patient preference, or bed capacity. NRD captures inpatient stays within a state and calendar year and does not observe out-of-hospital death. Residual confounding and complete-case selection may also affect estimates. The results do not establish that a different destination causes an adverse outcome or that changing destination would prevent one.

title: Different-Hospital First Readmission and Subsequent All-Cause Admission After Heart Failure Hospitalization
text:
Conclusion
Among adults with a heart failure index admission followed by a first all-cause readmission, readmission at a different hospital was associated with a modestly higher risk of the primary composite, with the strongest relative association observed for in-hospital death during the first readmission. These selected-cohort estimates describe associations and do not establish a causal effect of hospital destination.
